about: Scribal abbreviations in the manuscripts Milah collates.
A word is treated as an abbreviation because it carries one of the marks
scribes write them with -- geresh U+05F3, gershayim U+05F4, or the accents
U+059C and U+059E used for the same purpose -- so `stem` holds only the
letters. That is why a plain he is not mistaken for the divine name: the
mark is the signal, and comparisonKey throws it away, which is why the
table cannot live in hebrew_phrase_rules.json.
One entry covers every prefixed spelling: ל, ו and the other prefix
letters are peeled before the lookup and put back on the expansion, so
לה֞ resolves through the same row as ה֞.
A single-letter stem is also offered for a token with NO mark, because
copyists leave it off: Cochin's James writes the divine name as a bare ה
ten times. That is a suggestion only, never an alignment decision --
Sloane 237 writes a bare ה too, and there it is a detached definite
article. Longer stems are never matched unmarked, since an unmarked ישו
is just the bare form the phrase rules speak to.
Expansions are listed most likely first, and written POINTED. They are
stripped automatically when the Combined verse they would go into has no
vowel points, so a pointed edition gets אֱלֹהִים and an unpointed one
gets אלהים from this one entry. Write them pointed and let Milah reduce.
Numeric abbreviations (א׳ for one, י׳ב for twelve) are deliberately
absent: they expand to numbers rather than to words, and matching them
against a witness that spells the number out is a different problem.

entries.note: The divine name, left unwritten. Also matched without a mark.
Jesus. Sloane 237 writes it out as יְהוֹשֻׁעַ, Cochin abbreviates.

By the hand of. Written four ways across the witnesses — ע֞י and וע֞י in Revelation, ע״י in James, ע׳י in Matthew — and all four reach this one row, which is keyed on the letters alone. Sloane 237 says the same thing at Rev 1:1 with בְּיַד; the expansion here is the acronym's own letters, so the collation does not join the two readings.
